title: The Psalms of the Prophet's family
word: The Psalms of the Prophet's family
hook: Imam Ali Zayn al-Abidin's prayers, treasured by Shia Muslims and read by many others
tomorrow: what do you ask God for, when it comes to your parents?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Rumi's tomb in Konya, and a verse at the door that says, whoever you are, come again. Come, come again. Today, a new book: a book of prayers.

Some families keep a box of a grandmother's handwritten recipes, grease-spotted and annotated. Some keep her prayers. This book is that kind of inheritance. Ali, the son of Husayn and great-grandson of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, survived Karbala, a battle where his father and much of his family were killed. He's remembered as Zayn al-Abidin, the adornment of the worshippers. His prayers were gathered and kept. And tradition gives the book a striking nickname: the Psalms of the Prophet's family. Why psalms?
screen: `A GRANDMOTHER'S RECIPE BOX.` → `A SURVIVOR'S PRAYERS.` → `WHY CALL THEM PSALMS?`

segments.voice: The book is al-Sahifa al-Sajjadiyya, the pages of the one who prostrates. Shia Muslims treasure it, and many Sunni readers know and read it too. It's a book of whole prayers, for mornings and evenings, for sickness and repentance, for parents, neighbors and children, for when rain comes and when a debt weighs on you. Today's question is an old one: what do you say to God when your own words run out? The Sahifa's answer is, borrow some. Here's where a neighbor tradition says the same thing in its own words. Jews and Christians have prayed the Book of Psalms for every state of the heart. Psalm 130 opens, in the King James Version: Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD. That's what shared looks like: a family of old prayers, kept so that people in the depths have words ready. Muslims know the Psalms too; the Qur'an says God gave David the Zabur. And here's the honest difference. For Jews and Christians, the Psalms are scripture. For Muslims, the Sahifa isn't. Its prayers come from a holy man of the Prophet's family; the Qur'an alone is God's word. So the nickname names a likeness in use, not in rank. Two traditions, each with a book that lends words to people who've lost theirs. Prayers of the family.

segments.voice: Take a pen and copy one line of an old prayer you know by heart, from your own tradition or any you love, slowly, by hand. Notice which word your pen slows down on. Then read the line once, quietly, as if someone in your family had written it for you.
